question: A friend asks whether they should contribute to weatherly. What do you tell them?

options.text: Yes, the open PRs show people are engaged here.
options.explanation: The contributors are engaged, but the maintainer isn't. Open PRs only mean people tried — they say nothing about whether anyone is reviewing.

options.text: No, nobody seems to be reviewing PRs here.
options.explanation: The most recent merged PR is over a year old, four PRs are sitting open with no response, and the maintainer hasn't replied anywhere in almost a year. That's the clearest signal you can get.

options.text: Not sure — wait and see if #22 gets answered.
options.explanation: Issue #22 has been open for weeks with no reply. The silence is already your answer.

options.text: Yes, #5 is labelled good first issue.
options.explanation: Labels are set by maintainers and can be years old. This one was set about 16 months ago when the project was still active.

question: Which two signals are the strongest evidence that nobody will review your PR? (Select two)

options.text: There is no CONTRIBUTING.md.
options.explanation: Many small, healthy repos have no CONTRIBUTING.md. Absence of it alone doesn't signal abandonment.

options.text: The most recent merged PR is over a year old.
options.explanation: If nothing has been merged in over a year, there is no evidence the maintainer is still reviewing anything.

options.text: There are open PRs.
options.explanation: Busy, healthy repos have plenty of open PRs. Open PRs alone mean nothing — you need to look at whether they get responses.

options.text: The maintainer's last reply anywhere is almost a year old.
options.explanation: If the maintainer hasn't replied to any issue or PR in almost a year, there is no reason to expect they will reply to yours.

options.text: #5 has a good first issue label.
options.explanation: A label says nothing about whether anyone is reviewing. Labels are set once and rarely updated.

question: You've decided to contribute to weatherly. Which issue would you take?

options.text: #2 — Crash when the city isn't found.
options.explanation: This is a real, reproducible bug. But check the open PRs first — a fix has been sitting in PR #19 for 9 months with no response from the maintainer.

options.text: #5 — Add Fahrenheit option.
options.explanation: The label is about 16 months old and nobody is reviewing PRs. The change being small doesn't help if there's nobody to merge it.

options.text: #7 — IndexError when the weather list is empty.
options.explanation: A real bug, but someone claimed it in November and opened no PR since. Always ask before starting on a claimed issue.

options.text: #20 — API key invalid?
options.explanation: No steps, no version, no traceback. There is not enough information to reproduce this, let alone fix it.

options.text: None of these — I'd look for a different repo.
options.explanation: Every issue here has a problem: the repo is abandoned, fixes go unmerged, issues are claimed without follow-up, or reports lack enough information. The right call is to walk away.

question: You've reproduced issue #2 and want to fix it. What do you check first?

options.text: Whether a fix already exists somewhere in the repo.
options.explanation: PR #19 has had a correct fix sitting open for 9 months. Writing the same fix again would duplicate work that is already being ignored.

options.text: Whether your Python version matches the maintainer's.
options.explanation: Python version matters for compatibility, but it has no bearing on whether a fix already exists.

options.text: Whether the original reporter has contributed elsewhere.
options.explanation: The reporter's contribution history is irrelevant to whether you should open a duplicate fix.

options.text: How many reactions the issue has.
options.explanation: Reaction counts tell you how many people want a fix, not whether one already exists or whether anyone will review yours.

question: Issue #5 is labelled good first issue and the change is small. What is the real problem with taking it?

options.text: Small changes need a test first.
options.explanation: Tests are good practice, but they aren't the reason this issue is a bad pick.

options.text: Fahrenheit conversion is too hard for beginners.
options.explanation: The conversion itself is straightforward. Difficulty isn't the issue here.

options.text: Nobody is around to review it.
options.explanation: The maintainer wrote this label about 16 months ago when the project was active. A good first issue label only helps if someone is there to review the PR. There isn't.

options.text: The label only applies to documentation issues.
options.explanation: Good first issue applies to any kind of contribution. The label itself isn't the problem.

question: Issue #2 says parse_weather crashes when the city isn't found. You call it with a normal weather response and it works fine. What do you do next?

options.text: Mark it "Can't reproduce" — it works on my machine.
options.explanation: You didn't use the input described in the report. A normal response isn't the failing case.

options.text: Re-run it with the not-found response the report describes.
options.explanation: "Can't reproduce" only counts after you follow the reporter's exact steps. The crash happens with a not-found response, not a valid one.

options.text: Mark it "Reproduced" — the report is detailed enough to trust.
options.explanation: Trusting the report without running the steps isn't reproducing. You need to confirm it yourself.

options.text: Comment "works for me" and move on.
options.explanation: You tested the wrong input. This comment would be wrong and unhelpful.

question: You've decided weatherly isn't worth your time. What's the best next move?

options.text: Open a PR anyway to show interest.
options.explanation: A PR on an abandoned repo wastes your time and adds noise. It won't get reviewed.

options.text: Comment on #22 and wait for an answer.
options.explanation: Issue #22 has already been open for weeks with no reply. Waiting costs you weeks more on a project that's shown no signs of life.

options.text: Fork it and maintain it yourself.
options.explanation: Maintaining a fork is a months-long commitment. It's a valid path eventually, but not a first-contribution move.

options.text: Apply the same checks to a different project.
options.explanation: Moving on isn't failing — it's the skill this repo is here to teach. You just saved yourself weeks of work on a dead end.

question: Look at PR #16. Who is the conversation waiting on?

options.text: The maintainer.
options.explanation: The maintainer asked for a test. The author added it the same day and said so. Everything the author was asked to do is done — the ball is entirely in the maintainer's court.

options.text: The author, who still has changes to make.
options.explanation: The author replied the same day the changes were requested and confirmed the test was added. There is nothing left for them to do.

options.text: A second reviewer.
options.explanation: There is no mention of a second reviewer being required. The thread only involves the maintainer and the author.

options.text: Nobody — it's approved and ready to merge.
options.explanation: The maintainer never replied after the author added the test. It has not been approved.
